annotation.reasoning_summary: The layer maps discrete housing-block polygons for housing association holdings, not a full partition of the area, so PlainVectorRegion. The decisive entity rule is ObjectDS: each polygon is a real-world building/block asset with ownership and dwelling-count attributes, while the numeric fields are attributes rather than the main phenomenon.
Point features marking selected archaeological cesspit/find spots with address, description, and photos; this is a set of discrete objects/sites, not a measurement or event layer.

Point features mark selected archaeological find locations, not measurements or events. The decisive rule is object/location points with descriptive attributes and photos, so Geometry is PointDS and Entity is ObjectDS.

Polygons mark selected archaeological site areas rather than a full-area partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer represents bounded phenomenon zones/locations of archaeological finds, not reporting units or coverage, so PatchDS.
Polygon features are isolated park/area zones for barbecue restrictions, not a partition or reporting unit; this fits bounded selected phenomenon areas (patches).
Polygons are isolated protected conservation areas, not a complete tessellation. The layer represents selected bounded heritage zones, so PatchDS best fits.
Point locations record wild bee inventories/observations at specific places and years; the main phenomenon is occurrence of survey events, not point objects or amounts.
Point layer where each location represents a honey-bee hive/colony count; the main phenomenon is the numeric amount at points, so PointDS + AmountDS.
Polygon layer forms a near-complete tessellation of soil-quality zones with high shared boundaries. The main phenomenon is full-area categorical soil quality classification by zone, so CoverageDS.
Point features represent individual trees with species, planting year, owner, and manager attributes, so this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point features represent individual trees (named/numbered assets), so this is an object layer rather than amounts or events.
Point features represent individual trees as discrete real-world objects; numeric fields like plant year and radius are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Point features represent individual trees with species, tree number, owner/manager, and planting year; this is a discrete object layer, not measurements or events.
Point map of identifiable neighborhood compost initiatives at specific street locations; the points represent real-world objects/initiatives, not measurements or events.

Polygons mark selected camera-overlast areas rather than a full partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer is a bounded set of special zones/affected areas, not reporting units or objects, so PatchDS.
Point features represent individual trees (distinct, countable objects) with species and management attributes; this is an object layer, not amounts or events.
Point features represent distinct crowd-monitoring sensors/cameras, so the decisive rule is object points rather than measurements or events.

The layer shows selected cultural-historical areas and protected zones, not a full administrative/statistical partition. It is best treated as bounded phenomenon areas/patches rather than coverage or reporting units.
Point features mark distinct knotweed occurrences/observations; the numeric area field is an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

Point layer of ecological barrier/passages. The features are specific knelpunten/passage projects with status and realization year, so the main phenomenon is intervention/event-like occurrences rather than point objects or measurements.

Polygon features are isolated potential wind-energy areas, not a tessellating reporting unit or full coverage map. The decisive entity rule is patch: selected bounded zones with power/yield attributes, not objects or amount as the main phenomenon.
Point features represent vote locations, and the main mapped phenomenon is numeric election results shown by circle size and party vote counts/percentages, so this is PointDS with AmountDS.
Point layer of reported oak processionary caterpillar nests tied to ongoing status mutations and removal updates; the decisive rule is event/occurrence at locations rather than object inventory.

Polygon layer of pedicab restriction/permission areas; these are selected bounded zones with rules, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS for restricted/allowed areas.
Point features represent discrete pedicab and coach stand locations (standplaatsen), so this is a set of real-world objects rather than measurements, events, or amounts.
Point features represent individual non-residential address/building function objects (BAG verblijfsobjecten) with function attributes; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Polygons represent block-street function-mix classes, not a partition of the whole area; the decisive rule is full-area thematic classification (coverage) rather than reporting units or objects.
Neighborhood (Wijken/Buurtcombinaties) polygons form a tessellation of Amsterdam with strong shared boundaries; these are reporting/statistical units with codes and area attributes, so LatticeDS.

Neighborhood/buurtcombinatie polygons form a near-complete administrative partition with strong tessellation topology; they are reporting/statistical units with codes and area attributes, so LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete administrative partition with strong tessellation topology, and the layer is a reporting unit set (buurten/wijken) with codes and areas.
Neighborhood polygons with codes for buurt/buurtcombinatie/stadsdeel form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam; this is a reporting-unit tessellation, so VectorTessellation and LatticeDS.
City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition Amsterdam, and the polygon topology strongly supports tessellation; area is just an attribute, not the main phenomenon.

City districts are administrative reporting units forming a near-complete partition of Amsterdam; topology also shows adjacent polygons with shared boundaries. The numeric area field is an attribute, not the main phenomenon, so this is a lattice rather than amount.

The layer is a partition of Amsterdam areas/wards/neighbourhoods (“22 Areas”) with shared boundaries and no overlap, so it fits VectorTessellation. The polygons are reporting/administrative units with codes and names, so the entity is LatticeDS.

The layer is a near-complete partition of Amsterdam areas (buurten/wijken/gebieden/stadsdelen) with shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation applies. The polygons are reporting/statistical administrative units with codes and area attributes, so the entity is LatticeDS.

This is a tessellated set of Amsterdam practice areas/territorial units that partition the city area, so VectorTessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units with names, codes, and area values, which fits LatticeDS rather than AmountDS.

The layer is a set of named Amsterdam practice areas that together partition the city area, supported by shared boundaries and adjacency, so it is a tessellation. The polygons are reporting/statistical area units with codes and area attributes, so the entity is LatticeDS.

Polygon noise-contour zones for industrial noise; they are selected bounded impact areas rather than a complete reporting tessellation. The decisive entity rule is patch/selected phenomenon areas, with contour-like numeric labels as attributes.

Polygon noise bands are contour/interval zones (55-60, 60-65, etc.), not a full-area tessellation; classify as contour regions. The decisive entity rule is contour/isoline bands for Lden noise classes.

The layer shows noise-level classes (50-55 dB, 55-60 dB, etc.) as contour bands, not reporting units or objects. Polygons are class zones for isoline-like noise intervals, so ContourDS fits; despite many shared boundaries, the data are thematic noise bands rather than a full-area tessellation.

Noise contour polygons with dB classes and selection values; the layer represents contour bands/interval classes rather than reporting units or full coverage. Geometry follows the suggested region hint despite high adjacency because the theme is isolines/contours, not a tessellation.
Point layer of polling/stem locations; circle sizes encode vote counts and percentages, so the main phenomenon is numeric election amounts at points rather than the locations themselves.
Point features representing identifiable green roof locations/projects at addresses; numeric fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Land use polygons form a near-complete tessellation of the city area, and the codes classify each area by land-use category, so this is full-area thematic coverage.
Point features represent discrete historical buildings/archeological sites with names, functions, and dates; this is a set of identifiable objects, not amounts or events.

The layer represents Amsterdam boundary shapes used for area comparison (municipality/agglomeration/metropolitan region), so the polygons are discrete bounded objects rather than a reporting tessellation. The decisive entity rule is object: named bounded areas with an ID attribute, not a coverage or amount layer.
Polygon areas mark selected dog run / ban / restriction zones, not a full tessellation or reporting grid. The layer is best treated as bounded phenomenon patches with seasonal restrictions.

The layer shows selected bounded green areas and named green sites, not a full-area partition or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon zones; polygons are discrete green structure areas rather than a tessellation or coverage classification.

Point features represent individual trees (special/private elm trees), not measurements or events. The decisive rule is ObjectDS for distinct real-world assets; numeric fields like planting year and trunk diameter are attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Point locations mark discrete housing projects/buildings for youth and student housing; the numeric woning count is an attribute, not the main mapped phenomenon, so ObjectDS.
Points represent individual chestnut trees, with species and damage status as attributes; this is a discrete object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features sample a continuous environmental phenomenon; the layer is a drought/climate stress map with measured values (Maaiveld, GLG, GLG_maaiveld), so PointDS + PointMeasuresDS fits best.

Region polygons form a near-partition with high shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer is a flood-risk classification by probability/depth bands, which fits contour/interval-zone mapping.
Points mark fixed market locations; the layer is about identifiable markets as places/objects, not measurements or events.
Point features represent distinct named green monuments/treesites with monument status and dates, so this is an object layer; geometry is points.
Point features represent individual monumental trees; this is an object layer, not measurements or events.
Point layer of discrete monuments; each feature is a real-world heritage object, not a measurement or event. The decisive rule is object-based points.
Point locations mark current occurrence sites of protected wall flora; the map is primarily about presence of species at locations, not point measurements or amounts.
The layer shows NO2 measurement locations (meetpunten/meetstations) with 4-week concentration values, so the main phenomenon is sampled point measurements of air quality, not the points as objects.
Point layer of NO2 measurement locations; the main phenomenon is sampled air-quality measurements at points, so PointDS + PointMeasuresDS.

Polygon layer for the Oergeul primeval gulch, a bounded interpreted geological zone around Amsterdam rather than a reporting unit or full-area coverage. Sparse adjacency and low shared boundary support PlainVectorRegion; as a selected phenomenon zone, it fits PatchDS.
Point layer of bore/sounding locations; each point samples subsurface measurements (e.g., Top_Pleistoceen) rather than representing objects. Decisive rule: point measurements.
Polygons represent named development neighbourhoods/projects, not a full statistical tessellation; they are discrete bounded areas with object-like identity rather than coverage or reporting units.
Point features mark discrete public toilet facilities, with attributes describing type, opening hours, and fee; this is an object layer, not an amount or event.

Polygons are neighborhood-like areas with high shared boundaries, indicating a tessellation. The layer encodes overnight-policy conditions by area/category, so it is best treated as a full-area thematic coverage rather than objects or patches.

Polygon areas form a regional partition for parking standards by area; high shared boundaries and adjacency support tessellation, and the categorical field indicates a full-area thematic classification (coverage).
Discrete named park and green-space polygons with area attributes; they are managed objects, not a reporting tessellation or full-area coverage.

Postcode4 areas are reporting/administrative units that partition the city, and the topology hints strongly support tessellation (high shared boundaries, many adjacencies, low overlap). The numeric area field is auxiliary, so the main entity is a lattice/reporting-unit layer.
Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units that broadly partition the city, and the topology strongly supports a tessellation (high shared boundaries and adjacency).
Postcode6 polygons are reporting units that together form a near-complete tessellation of the area; the decisive rule is tessellation + reporting-unit lattice.
Line geometries represent road/transport infrastructure networks (plusnetten en hoofdnetten); the layer is about connected route systems, not individual objects or amounts.
Layer depicts Amsterdam plus/head networks for pedestrian priority, so the main phenomenon is a connected transport/infrastructure network; polygons are discrete route/zone areas, not a tessellation.
Point layer of named locations/cameras/sensors; main phenomenon is identifiable objects with privacy statements, not measurements or events.
Point layer of privacy-related investigations/analyses at locations; the decisive rule is point geometry plus event-like occurrences/activities rather than objects or measurements.
Point features mark distinct camera/sensor locations for the car fleet scan; this is a set of identifiable objects, not a measurement or amount layer.
Point layer of election polling/stem locations where the main mapped phenomenon is vote counts and percentages at each location, so PointDS + AmountDS.

Polygons mark selected rainproof drainage problem areas rather than a full tessellation; the layer is a set of bounded affected zones. The key attribute is a categorical drainage possibility (possible/not possible), so PatchDS fits better than coverage or lattice.

Polygons are isolated hydro-unit solution areas, not a full tessellation or reporting grid; the layer represents selected Rainproof problem/solution zones from the map description, so PatchDS fits best.

The polygons are isolated bottleneck zones, not a complete partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer marks selected rainwater-problem areas from model analysis, which fits PatchDS rather than reporting units or coverage.

Polygons mark selected rainproof problem areas linked to modeled water-overstreet nuisance, not a full-area partition or reporting units. The decisive rule is bounded phenomenon patch, so PlainVectorRegion + PatchDS.
Point features represent identifiable religious buildings/locations with names and addresses, so this is an object layer rather than measurements or events.
Line dataset about sidewalk segments; the main mapped phenomenon is sidewalk width/comfort as a numeric magnitude on linear features, so LineDS + AmountDS.
Line geometry with street/route segments for mopeds on the roadway; the layer maps a transport/road network decision (verkeersbesluit), not point objects or amounts.
Point features represent discrete public sports/playground facilities (basketball, tennis, etc.), so this is an object layer; the surface area is just an attribute, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point locations for city farming sites; each feature is a distinct real-world place/facility, not a measurement or event.

Polygons represent discrete named city-farming sites/terrains with addresses and websites, not a partition of Amsterdam, so PlainVectorRegion. The main phenomenon is identifiable objects (gardens/plots), not amount or coverage, so ObjectDS.
Point features mark where the city pilot facilitated placements over time; the decisive rule is event/occurrence at locations, with year indicating temporal unfolding rather than object inventory.
Major streets are a connected road/route system represented by LineString features, so the decisive rule is network infrastructure on lines.
Line geometry with transport network semantics; the layer is explicitly district heating/cooling transport lines, so NetworkDS is decisive.

Layer depicts district heating/cooling network areas buffered into polygons, not a full partition; the decisive meaning is connected heat/cold infrastructure, so NetworkDS with PlainVectorRegion geometry.

Polygons are discrete project/plan areas for housing development, not a full tessellation; the layer represents selected strategic plan zones with housing-plan counts as attributes, so PatchDS fits best.
Point locations of named local food initiatives and farms; the decisive rule is object points rather than amounts or events.
Line geometry and metadata describe tram/metro routes and stations as a transport network; decisive rule: network system.
Line geometries represent Amsterdam tram/metro routes and stations network; the decisive rule is connected transport infrastructure, so NetworkDS.
Point features represent tram stops and metro stations, while the layer’s purpose is the transit/station network rather than point objects or amounts.

Point features represent tram stops and metro stations, and the metadata explicitly describes the tram/metro network and lines. Classified as PointDS with NetworkDS because the main phenomenon is a transport route system, not point objects or amounts.
Point layer of identifiable traffic-light-controlled intersections; the points represent distinct real-world objects, not measurements or events.
Line geometries represent road links in a traffic prognosis network, and the main mapped phenomenon is traffic volume/intensity on each link, so this is LineDS with AmountDS.
Point layer of stemlocaties (polling places) with vote totals and turnout values; the main phenomenon is numeric election results at locations, so PointDS + AmountDS.
Point features represent individual trees (tree replacement layer); numeric fields are object attributes like ID, planting year, and size classes, so this is ObjectDS, not AmountDS.
Point layer of Amsterdam traffic information system assets; each point is a distinct managed object/facility, not a measurement or event.
Point layer of identifiable traffic information system installations; metadata says clicking an object shows more info, so these are discrete objects, not measurements or events.

Point features mark discrete bird nesting/breeding locations at addresses; the main phenomenon is identifiable object-like observation sites, not a numeric amount layer. The yearly counts are attributes, so object over amount.
Point features represent individual benches in Vondelpark, a set of identifiable real-world objects; the adoption status is just an attribute, so this is ObjectDS on PointDS geometry.

Line features represent street segments/sidewalk sections, and the main mapped phenomenon is walkability/space/traffic intensity classes along those lines rather than the lines as a network object; this fits line-based amount-like thematic values.

Point features represent discrete wall art objects at buildings, not measurements or events. The decisive rule is object-in-points: each feature is a countable artwork with descriptive attributes like title, artist, year, and address.

Polygons form a near-complete area partition with high shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer maps Amsterdam welstand categories (area-wide regulatory classes), which is a full-area thematic coverage.

The polygons form a near-complete partition of Amsterdam's wellstand system areas, supported by high shared boundaries and adjacency; the layer is a full-area thematic classification of welstand levels, so CoverageDS.
Point features mark WWII attack/incidence locations with dates and descriptions; the main phenomenon is events/occurrences at places, not objects or measurements.

The layer maps housing plan polygons with main numeric totals (Totaal, housing counts) for discrete project areas, so the phenomenon is amount-based. The polygons are project footprints/selected areas rather than a full tessellation, despite some adjacency, so PlainVectorRegion + AmountDS.
Point features mark discrete self-build plot/project locations with names and contact info, so this is a point object layer rather than a measurement or amount layer.

Polygons are selected building/dak footprints showing where solar panels are possible, not a full-area tessellation. The layer is a bounded phenomenon/zone map with categorical suitability, so PatchDS.
Point features represent solar-panel systems with numeric panel count and watt-peak capacity as the main mapped phenomenon; this is a point amount layer, not just objects with attributes.
Point layer of named swimming and play-water locations; the decisive rule is object vs amount, and these are discrete facilities/places rather than measurements or events.
